title: Roman Concrete
objective: After this level you can explain what made Roman concrete so durable.
summary: Lime and volcanic ash made a concrete that set underwater and shaped domes. Lumps of lime even helped it heal its own cracks.

cards.headline: Romans built harbors out in the sea, with concrete that set underwater.
cards.body: How do you make something harden while it’s soaking wet? The secret came out of a volcano.

cards.headline: Ash and lime
cards.body: Roman concrete mixed lime with volcanic ash, called pozzolana, plus chunks of rock or brick. The ash is named after Pozzuoli, near Naples, where it was dug. It was the key ingredient: concrete made with it could set even underwater. So Romans could do something that sounds like a terrible idea, putting fresh concrete into the sea, and build harbors there.
cards.callout: Pozzolana: volcanic ash from near Naples

cards.headline: New shapes, hidden core
cards.body: Concrete didn’t just survive the sea. It let Romans build arches, vaults and domes on a scale never seen before. You’d rarely notice it, though. Walls were usually faced with brick or stone, so the concrete core was hidden from view. Rome showed you the neat outfit and kept the muscle underneath.

cards.context: A 2023 study found that lumps of lime in the mix could react with water to seal cracks, helping the concrete last. Water, the enemy of most buildings, was helping these ones heal.

cards.headline: Concrete: set
learned: Concrete mixed lime and volcanic ash
It made domes and vaults possible

questions.prompt: What volcanic ingredient went into Roman concrete?
questions.explanation: Roman concrete mixed lime with volcanic ash called pozzolana.

questions.prompt: Why could Romans build harbors out in the sea?

options.label: They drained the sea with pumps

questions.prompt: From Level 46: Augustus boasted he found Rome a city of brick and left it a city of what?
questions.explanation: Augustus claimed he left Rome a city of marble; much of it was marble facing over concrete and brick.
